contributions: Systematic introduction of 33 graph theory concepts needed for graph ML, organized from basic definitions (nodes, edges, adjacency matrices) through advanced topics (isomorphism, homomorphism)
Unified framing of three diverse application domains—drug discovery, social recommendation, and fraud detection—as graphs sharing a common representational structure
Explicit connection between adjacency matrix operations and the core message-passing mechanism underlying all GNNs
Discussion of two robust empirical regularities in real-world networks: logarithmic average path length (small-world) and power-law degree distributions (scale-free)
limitations: Graph isomorphism is described as an open problem in computational complexity with no known polynomial-time algorithm and no proof of NP-hardness, placing it in a complexity limbo. Dense adjacency matrix storage is impractical for large real-world graphs due to sparsity. The chapter acknowledges (but defers to later chapters) that aggregating over hubs with thousands of neighbors is computationally very different from typical nodes, motivating sampling strategies. Most GNNs cannot distinguish certain pairs of non-isomorphic graphs, a limitation addressed in Chapter 9.
methods: The chapter is expository rather than empirical. It defines graphs formally as pairs G=(V,E), introduces adjacency matrices and sparse edge-list representations, derives node degree and in-/out-degree for directed graphs, and defines paths, cycles, connected components, and graph diameter. BFS and DFS are described as algorithmic foundations. Three motivating real-world problems (molecular prediction, music recommendation, fraud detection) are presented to demonstrate the unifying power of the graph formalism. The text also covers special graph types (bipartite, heterogeneous, multigraph, weighted, attribute), substructures (subgraphs, ego networks, cliques, trees, planar graphs), and the computational complexity status of graph isomorphism.
results: The chapter cites that the ogbn-arxiv graph has 169,343 nodes, whose dense adjacency matrix would require approximately 28.7 billion entries. Real-world networks have average shortest path lengths growing logarithmically with n, with the Facebook network of roughly 3 billion users having an average distance of approximately 3.5 hops. Power-law degree distributions follow P(k) proportional to k^(-gamma), with gamma typically between 2 and 3 for real networks. In the Erdős–Rényi model G(n,c/n), a giant connected component emerges when c > 1. The text notes that real networks have average degrees typically between 2 and 100, making sparse representations essential.
tldr: This introductory chapter establishes the mathematical language of graphs and real-world network properties as foundational prerequisites for graph neural networks, covering definitions, representations, degree distributions, connectivity, special graph types, and two consistent empirical regularities: small-world structure and scale-free degree distributions.
